headline_en: Two young Italy-based expatriates killed in motorcycle accident in Chandpur
summary_en: Two young Bangladeshis living in Italy, home on leave for Ramadan and Eid, died when their motorcycle went under a covered van at Puranbazar, Chandpur town, on the night of Monday 3 March 2025. The van driver fled; locals seized the van. Police say legal action is being taken after investigation.

facts.statement: Italy-based Bangladeshi Avi Dewan (17), son of Md. Abdus Salam Dewan of Merkatiz Road, Puranbazar, Chandpur, and his cousin Niloy (18), son of Md. Selim Mia of Gharisa, Shariatpur, also living in Italy, died after their motorcycle fell under a goods-carrying covered van in front of Puranbazar Girls' School, Chandpur, at about 10:15 pm on Monday (3 March 2025). Avi died on the spot; Niloy died on the way to Chandpur Government General Hospital.

Avi Dewan came home from Italy on 11 February (2025) and Niloy on 18 February to spend Ramadan and Eid leave in Bangladesh; they were killed while overtaking a bicycle at speed on the way to Natun Bazar, Chandpur.

The covered-van driver fled after the accident; local people seized the van. The officer-in-charge of Chandpur Model Police Station, Md. Bahar Mia, said police were sent to the spot and legal action is being taken after investigation.
facts.source_in_article: Chandpur Model Police Station OC Md. Bahar Mia

headline_en: 10 Bangladeshis taken to Russia via Saudi Arabia and sold to a 'Sultan'
summary_en: CID arrested a woman (named both Fabiha Jerin and Tamanna in the article), a partner of Dream Home Travels and Tours Ltd, at Dhaka airport as she was about to flee to Nepal, over a ring that trafficked 10 Bangladeshis to Russia with promises of jobs paying 2 to 2.5 lakh taka a month. The victims were sent to Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas, then to Russia, sold to a 'Sultan' and handed to Russian soldiers, trained and forced to fight against Ukraine; one died and one was badly injured. Another group of 10 refused to go on from Saudi Arabia and had their passports taken; CID is trying to bring them home.

facts.statement: CID arrested a woman named Fabiha Jerin from the Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport area in Dhaka on Wednesday night (5 February 2025), just before she was about to flee to Nepal, for alleged involvement in trafficking people from Bangladesh to Russia. The CID press release names the arrested woman as Tamanna; the article uses both names.
facts.source_in_article: CID media wing Special Superintendent Jasim Uddin Khan; CID press release

facts.statement: Tamanna, the arrested woman, is a partner in a company called Dream Home Travels and Tours Limited and a member of a human trafficking ring; CID says she confessed her involvement. Her brother Tuhin, currently in Russia, motivated ordinary people to go to the war.
The ring promised 10 Bangladeshis jobs in Russia paying 2 to 2.5 lakh taka a month. Instead of the promised work, they were given military training and forced to fight in the war against Ukraine.

Route used by the ring: the 10 people were first sent to Saudi Arabia on Umrah visas, made to perform Umrah, then taken to Russia and sold to a 'Sultan', who handed them as slaves to Russian soldiers.
In the war, Humayun Kabir of Singra police station area, Natore, was killed and Aminul of Keraniganj, Dhaka, was seriously injured.

Akram Hossain of Palash police station area, Narsingdi, one of the 10 trafficked, escaped from the training camp and returned to Bangladesh by his own arrangement on 26 January (2025), then contacted the families of other victims.
On Tuesday (4 February 2025) Jhumu Akter, wife of the war-injured Aminul, filed a case at Banani police station in Dhaka; the arrest at Shahjalal airport followed from that case's investigation.

Another group of 10 trafficked Bangladeshis is in Saudi Arabia; they refused to go on to Russia on learning they would be forced to fight, so their passports were taken away. Without passports they cannot work and cannot return home. CID is trying to bring them back.

headline_en: Thai visa from home within 10 days
summary_en: The Royal Thai Embassy in Dhaka announced on 15 December 2024 that from 2 January 2025 Bangladeshi ordinary passport holders can apply online for an e-visa and get it within 10 working days; official passport holders can travel visa-free from 19 December. Existing application centres stop taking applications from 24 December. The article notes India has stopped tourist visas for Bangladeshis since the July 2024 uprising.

facts.statement: From 2 January (2025) the Royal Thai Embassy offers e-visas to Bangladeshi ordinary passport holders: they apply online and should get the visa within 10 days; announced in a notice by the Thai Embassy in Dhaka on Monday 15 December (2024).

The Thai e-visa process has 6 steps done online at home: open an account in your own name, fill the application form, upload required attachments and documents, pay the set visa fee, then wait. The result is sent by e-mail; processing takes 10 working days, so the visa confirmation documents arrive by e-mail in roughly 2 weeks.
The copy of the Thai e-visa sent by e-mail must be printed and shown to immigration on entering Thailand.
Thai e-visa website: https://www.thaievisa.go.th/
Because of the e-visa, the Thai Embassy stops accepting visa applications at the existing application centre from 24 December (2024).
Bangladeshi official (government) passport holders can travel to Thailand without a visa from 19 December (2024); diplomatic passport holders have had visa-free travel since 2018.
Thailand's e-visa has already been launched at 69 Thai embassies.
Since the July 2024 uprising India has kept tourist visas closed for Bangladeshis; medical and higher-education visas are being given, but on a limited scale.

headline_en: Delivery of expatriate workers' passports to start from 10 December: Law Adviser
summary_en: Law Adviser Asif Nazrul said on 20 November 2024 that delivery of renewed passports to non-resident Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia and other countries is expected to start from 10 December, as foil paper for printing passports is being brought in. He said workers abroad prefer MRP passports over e-passports, though MRP is outdated and the national goal is to move to e-passports; there is no crisis in issuing e-passports.

facts.statement: Law Adviser Asif Nazrul said on Wednesday evening (20 November 2024) at a press briefing at the Foreign Service Academy, Dhaka, that delivery of passports to non-resident Bangladeshis, especially migrant workers in Malaysia and other countries waiting for passport renewal, is expected to start from 10 December (2024). The Home Secretary and Director General of the Department of Immigration and Passports told him foil paper for printing passports is being brought in.
Migrants are having passport problems not only in Malaysia but in many Middle Eastern countries, according to the Law Adviser, who said many workers message him with complaints.

There are two kinds of Bangladeshi passport: e-passport and MRP (machine-readable passport). The Law Adviser said there is no crisis in issuing e-passports, but migrant workers do not want e-passports and want MRP passports; MRP is outdated ('backdated') and the national goal is to move from MRP to e-passports.

headline_en: 'I was 15 days under the open sky by the sea with wife and child': Lebanon returnee Hossain
summary_en: 54 Bangladeshis, including Mohammad Hossain's family, returned from war-hit Lebanon on a government-arranged flight on 21 October 2024 and were received at Dhaka airport by Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul. Returnees described Israeli bombing everywhere in Lebanon and living on the seashore. Asif Nazrul said about 100,000 Bangladeshis are in Lebanon, 1,800 have asked to return, the government will bring back all who want, and 17 crore 55 lakh (taka) has been spent so far.

facts.statement: Because of the war, 54 Bangladeshis returned from Lebanon on Monday 21 October 2024 under a Bangladesh government initiative; their flight landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at 5:55 pm, and they were received by Professor Asif Nazrul, adviser to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment. The article links this as the first phase of returns from Lebanon.
About one lakh (100,000) Bangladeshi migrants live in Lebanon, of whom 1,800 had expressed a wish to return home as of 21 October 2024; the adviser said this number could rise or fall.

The interim government will spend whatever money is needed to bring migrants back from Lebanon and will bring back everyone who wants to return; 17 crore 55 lakh has already been spent (currency not stated), according to the adviser.

Returnees told the adviser that Israeli forces' attacks were so severe that people who moved from south Lebanon to north Lebanon were still attacked; there is no place in Lebanon where they can keep safe, and many are living in inhumane conditions on the seashore.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul, citing returnees

facts.statement: Returnee Mohammad Hossain said four or five buildings next to the building where he lived were flattened, Israeli aircraft were always in the sky, and no place in Lebanon is safe; he spent 15 days with his wife and child under the open sky by the sea, where it was very cold and windy.
Returnee Lipi Akter said that even as they were boarded onto the plane she heard bombs falling and the plane shook; another bomb was dropped before take-off.
Lebanon returnees asked the government to bring back quickly all who want to return, to rehabilitate returnees, and to arrange work for them in Bangladesh or send them to another country.
facts.source_in_article: returnees Mohammad Hossain and Mohammad Rajon

headline_en: Studying in Taiwan: part-time jobs and scholarships, IELTS or TOEFL score needed
summary_en: A study-abroad guide (sourced to UNB News) on higher education in Taiwan for Bangladeshis: eligibility, English requirements, intakes, documents, the resident visa process via the Taipei Economic and Cultural Center in New Delhi (no Taiwan mission in Bangladesh), visa and authentication fees, scholarships, study and living costs, part-time work rules (20 hours a week with ARC and work permit), and the route to jobs and permanent residence.

facts.statement: Eligibility for study in Taiwan: undergraduate needs a pass in higher secondary or equivalent diploma; master's needs a bachelor's degree; doctoral needs a master's degree.

Learning Mandarin or Chinese is not required for bachelor's, master's or doctoral study in Taiwan, as there are English-taught courses; English proficiency needed is IELTS 5.5 to 6 or TOEFL iBT 71 to 80. Learning Mandarin is important for cheaper study options and scholarships.

Taiwanese universities admit in September (fall) and February (spring); fall has the most course choices. Applications are online through each institution's own application platform; deadlines and conditions must be checked on the university websites.

Documents for admission to a Taiwanese university: higher secondary or equivalent diploma certificate, academic transcript, online application form, passport-size photo, national ID card, passport, IELTS or TOEFL score, application fee (varies by university; some accept applications free), several recommendation letters, proof of financial solvency, study plan, statement of purpose, and a research proposal for PhD.
Bangladeshi students going to Taiwan for higher study must apply for a resident visa, which allows stay of more than 180 days (6 months) and is valid for 1 year; it can be renewed after one year.

Taiwan resident visa application: enter details at https://visawebapp.boca.gov.tw and upload scanned documents; after submitting, download and print the application, making sure it carries a barcode, and sign it in the marked place.

For Bangladeshi passport holders the key document for a Taiwan resident visa is a guarantee letter from a person living in Taiwan inviting the applicant. The applicant downloads the Letter of Guarantee form (from the rocaiwan.org website, link printed in the article) and sends it to the inviter, who fills, scans and e-mails it back and keeps the original. TECC (Taipei Economic and Cultural Center) then gives the applicant a visa number, which the applicant passes to the inviter; the inviter then submits the original guarantee letter to Taiwan's BOCA (Bureau of Consular Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs). After the consular office verifies it and informs TECC, the visa is issued. Guarantee verification takes at least seven working days.

Documents for a Taiwan student resident visa: signed online visa application form; request letter stating purpose, type and length of study; two recent passport photos on white background (3.4 x 4.5 cm); valid passport with more than six months' validity and at least two blank pages; admission offer letter from a Taiwanese university; photocopies of latest degree certificate and transcripts (originals to show at the counter; must be translated into English); guarantee letter; health certificate issued within three months; proof of finances (sponsor's income tax return and last three months' bank statements, covering at least six continuous months of living costs); scholarship certificate stating period and amount if any; study plan; language certificate if applicable; police criminal record certificate if applicable. These documents must be authenticated by an ROC (Republic of China) foreign mission.
Taiwan has no embassy in Bangladesh; visa documents are submitted and the interview held at the Taiwan consular office in India: 34, Paschimi Marg, Vasant Vihar, New Delhi-110057, India.

At the Taiwan office in New Delhi, documents are taken, fingerprints and photo are recorded for biometric registration, visa fees are collected and an ICR (Invoice cum Receipt) is given, which must be brought when collecting the passport with visa. Resident visa processing takes a total of eight working days; original documents are returned after processing.

Document authentication fees for a Taiwan visa: 400 NTD (1,498 taka) per original and 200 NTD (749 taka) per copy, ready after two working days; for same-day (one day), 600 NTD (2,246 taka) per original and 300 NTD (1,123 taka) per copy (article uses 1 NTD = 3.74 taka).

Taiwan resident visa fee: single entry 2.2 thousand NTD or 5.7 thousand Indian rupees (about 8,137 taka); multiple entry 4.4 thousand NTD or 11.4 thousand rupees (16,275 taka) (article uses 1 rupee = 1.43 taka).

Taiwan scholarships: Taiwan Scholarship Program gives a monthly stipend of 25,000 NTD (93,582 taka); Taiwan ICDF Scholarship gives 12,000 NTD (44,920 taka) a month for undergraduates, about 18,000 NTD (67,379 taka) for master's and 20,000 NTD (74,866 taka) for PhD; Huayu Enrichment Scholarship gives 25,000 NTD (93,582 taka) a month.

Study costs in Taiwan: undergraduate about 53.2 thousand to 84 thousand NTD a year (about 199,142 to 314,435 taka); master's 33 thousand to 168 thousand NTD a year (123,527 to 628,870 taka); PhD tuition 96 thousand to 2 lakh NTD a year (359,354 to 748,654 taka).

Living costs in Taiwan: foreign students spend on average 3,000 NTD (11,230 taka) a month on groceries; eating out at a local market costs at least 60 NTD (225 taka); city bus monthly pass 500 NTD (1,872 taka); Taipei Metro MRT monthly fare 700 NTD (2,621 taka); a one-bedroom apartment outside the city centre about 12,000 NTD (44,920 taka) a month; utilities 2,000 NTD (7,487 taka) a month.

International students in Taiwan may work up to 20 hours a week during the semester, but need two things: an Alien Resident Certificate (ARC) card, the foreign student ID and proof of legal residence, which students should apply for first on arrival; and a work permit applied for from the Workforce Development Agency, usually valid for one semester or six months and to be re-applied for before it expires.

Part-time jobs for students in Taiwan include restaurant work and sales assistant (non-academic) and research or teaching assistant, translator and language teaching at a cram school (academic); they pay 120 to 400 NTD (450 to 1,498 taka) an hour.
After at least five continuous years in Taiwan a person can apply for permanent residence, with no criminal record in that period, skills in a specific job, and a contribution to national prosperity.
A fresh graduate in Taiwan may stay an extra six months after graduation to find a job or start a business, and can apply for a further six-month extension if more time is needed.

Average annual salary for full-time jobs in Taiwan is about 1 lakh to 6.7 lakh NTD (about 374,327 to 2,507,991 taka); jobs include doctor, pharmacist, nurse, marketing manager, salesperson, electrical, mechanical and civil engineer.

headline_en: 26 more Bangladeshis return from UAE after pardon
summary_en: 26 more Bangladeshis jailed in the UAE for protesting in support of the anti-discrimination student movement returned home on 13 September 2024 on an IndiGo flight after a pardon. The UAE had arrested and jailed 57 Bangladeshis in July; President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan pardoned all 57 at Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus's request, and 31 had already returned in three batches. BRAC Migration Programme is giving transport and other support and will work with the Wage Earners' Welfare Board on reintegration.

facts.statement: In July 2024 the UAE government arrested 57 Bangladeshis for protesting in the UAE in support of the anti-discrimination student movement and sentenced them to jail terms of various lengths.

At Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus's request, UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan ordered a pardon for the 57 Bangladeshis and their jail sentences were withdrawn; 31 returned home in three batches, and the remaining 26 returned on Friday 13 September 2024 at 3:05 pm on an IndiGo Airlines flight.

BRAC Migration Programme, through the Probashi Kallyan (expatriate welfare) desk, is giving the 26 returnees from the UAE necessary support including transport costs; the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's Wage Earners' Welfare Board and BRAC will work on their economic and social reintegration, providing psychosocial and economic support according to their needs.
facts.source_in_article: Shariful Hasan, Associate Director, BRAC Migration Programme and Youth Platform

headline_en: Expatriate Bangladeshis played a unique role in the student-people uprising
summary_en: A diaspora feature on protests by Bangladeshis abroad during the July 2024 uprising, in the UK, Europe, North America, Asia and the Middle East. It notes that public gatherings are banned in Middle Eastern countries; UAE courts sentenced 57 Bangladeshis for street protests (53 to 10 years, 1 to 11 years, 3 to life), and arrests were also reported in Saudi Arabia and the Maldives. Migrants announced a remittance stoppage after the internet shutdown from 17 July.

facts.statement: In Middle Eastern countries any kind of public meeting or rally is banned, according to the article.

UAE authorities detained many Bangladeshis for street protests over student killings in Bangladesh; a UAE court convicted 57 Bangladeshis: 53 got 10 years each, 1 got 11 years and 3 got life imprisonment.
Several Bangladeshis were reported arrested in Saudi Arabia over protests during the July 2024 movement; arrests of protesting Bangladeshis were also reported in the Maldives.
After internet shutdown in Bangladesh from 17 July 2024, migrants were cut off from families, and announced they would stop sending remittances to Bangladesh.
The article says more than 1.5 crore (15 million) Bangladeshis live abroad across the world.

summary_en: A short jobs-section listicle on a 2024 ranking (source not named) of the 10 best countries for work environment, based on job opportunities, work-life balance, quality of life and expatriate-worker-friendly policies, with the sectors said to have openings in each.

facts.statement: A list published in 2024 (source not named) ranks the best countries for work environment, based on job opportunities, work-life balance, quality of life and expatriate-worker-friendly policies: 1 New Zealand, 2 Netherlands, 3 South Korea, 4 Australia, 5 Germany, 6 Brazil, 7 Denmark, 8 Botswana, 9 Canada, 10 Cambodia.
New Zealand is said to have many jobs in agriculture, tourism and technology.
The Netherlands is said to have job opportunities in the technology industry.
South Korea is said to have many jobs in electronics, automotive and technology.
Australia is said to pay high wages, with many jobs in finance, healthcare and mining in Sydney and Melbourne.
Germany is said to have many jobs for expatriates in engineering, automotive and finance.
Brazil is said to have many jobs in agriculture, energy and tourism in Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.
Denmark is said to offer expatriate workers benefits through a strong social welfare system, with jobs in education, pharmaceuticals and technology.
Botswana is said to offer expatriates work in agriculture, mining and tourism.
Canada is said to have wide openings in healthcare, with Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal frequently calling for workers in finance, technology and healthcare.
Cambodia is said to be gaining popularity among expatriate workers for jobs.

headline_en: Monetary policy off target due to money printing and dollar sales
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank's July-December monetary policy review shows the policy nearly missed its targets because of money printing and dollar sales from reserves. The article notes remittances are rising because of a concession in the dollar rate; the new monetary policy (posted 18 July 2024) fixes the dollar at 117 taka with a hint of moving to a market rate, and expects offshore banking, foreign-currency accounts for returnees and higher remittances to ease exchange-rate pressure.

facts.statement: Remittance inflows are increasing because of a concession on the dollar price, according to the reporter, while Bangladesh still faces dollar and taka shortages and pressure on reserves.
In the monetary policy posted on its website on 18 July 2024, Bangladesh Bank announced keeping the US dollar price at 117 taka, hinting it will become market-based in future.

Bangladesh Bank's new monetary policy says offshore banking, the opening of foreign-currency accounts by people returning from abroad, and higher remittance inflows will reduce pressure on the exchange rate and increase reserves.

headline_en: 'Came to Malaysia, no work in three months, and Eid is here'
summary_en: On Eid ul-Azha (17 June 2024), the article reports that nearly 4.75 lakh workers went to Malaysia in a year and a half, spending on average more than 5 lakh taka each, and some got no job. A worker from Shibchar who paid 4.9 lakh taka has had no work for three months. Many Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia get no leave on Eid, work long shifts, and are not even given time for Eid prayers.

facts.statement: In about a year and a half up to June 2024, nearly 4.75 lakh (পৌনে পাঁচ লাখ) Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia, spending on average more than 5 lakh taka each; some of them did not get jobs. Several lakh more Bangladeshi workers were already in Malaysia.

Md. Rajib of Shibchar, Madaripur, went to Malaysia about three months before 17 June 2024 after spending 4 lakh 90 thousand taka, but had not got a job; he was staying with an uncle (খালু) in Kuala Lumpur for food and lodging and could not send any money home.

Migrants say a large share of workers in Malaysia get no holiday even on Eid day and go to work instead of Eid prayers. Md. Raihan Kashem, in Malaysia for six to seven years and working at a supershop in Malacca, said he gets no leave on Eid and is not given time even to pray, in any year.

In the Facebook group 'Malaysia Kajer Khobor' (মালয়েশিয়া কাজের খবর), migrant Iftekhar Ahmed wrote he was going to duty on Eid day, working 10 am to 10 pm, and was refused a single day off; another migrant, Md. Ashraful Ahmed, replied that he works 6 am to 8 pm.

Migrant online communities named in the article: Facebook group 'Malaysia Kajer Khobor' (মালয়েশিয়া কাজের খবর) and Facebook page 'Malaysiaprobashi Bangladeshi' (মালয়েশিয়াপ্রবাসী বাংলাদেশি), admin Rakib Rana.

headline_en: We are Kuddus who survived the jaws of tiger and crocodile
summary_en: An opinion column by Anisul Hoque praising Sundarbans forest workers, migrant workers and garment workers for keeping Bangladesh's economy afloat. It mentions dangerous irregular routes (rubber boats across the Mediterranean from Morocco, hostage camps in jungles, freezing in refrigerated vehicles), states that 18,166 migrant bodies came home in 2018-2022 with one in five dying in road accidents, and that workers sleep 14 to a room to save money.

facts.statement: In the five years 2018 to 2022, the bodies of 18,166 Bangladeshi migrants were brought home; one in five of them died in road accidents, according to the columnist.

Young Bangladeshis seeking work try to reach Europe by crossing the Mediterranean in rubber boats from countries like Morocco and die; others fall into traffickers' hands and are held hostage in jungles or die on the way to the Far East, or freeze to death crossing borders in refrigerated vehicles, according to the columnist.
Migrant workers sleep crammed 14 to a room, going without food themselves, to save dollars to send home, according to the columnist.

headline_en: Foreign Minister stresses economic diplomacy to strengthen ties with South Korea
summary_en: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud met South Korean Ambassador Park Young-sik in Dhaka on 20 March 2024 to discuss trade, investment and skilled-worker exports. He thanked Korea for raising the EPS quota for Bangladeshi workers. The ambassador said Bangladesh could not fill its 10,200 quota last year because of language-learning problems, and the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry has designated two TTCs where Korean trainers can give language and technical training.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 20 March 2024 Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud thanked South Korea for increasing the quota for Bangladeshi skilled workers under Korea's Employment Permit System (EPS) scheme, at a meeting with South Korean Ambassador Park Young-sik in Dhaka.
Bangladesh could not fill its EPS quota of 10,200 workers for South Korea last year (2023) because of problems with language learning, according to South Korean Ambassador Park Young-sik.

To solve the language problem, Bangladesh's Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment has designated two Technical Training Centres (TTCs) in Bangladesh where Korean trainers can give the necessary language and technical training for South Korea-bound workers.
